title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 19 November 2026 (week 47) - GOV.UK

analysis.time: The report was published on 19 November 2026, and the data it references covers up to week 46 of 2026 (9 November to 15 November 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: The report focuses on England, with specific mention of populations aged 75 years and over, those under 75 with weakened immune systems, and age groups such as 85 years and over.
analysis.event: The report details the surveillance findings for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), influenza, and RSV in England during week 46 of 2026. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, influenza activity increased, and RSV activity also increased.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 17 November 2026, there were 1,826 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases in hospital settings during week 46. Influenza positivity increased to 11.4% compared to 8.3% in the previous week, with influenza A positivity at 10.1% and influenza B at 0.3%. RSV activity increased, with acute bronchiolitis ED attendances rising.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report indicates that influenza activity is above baseline levels, and a briefing note has been issued to the NHS. The data is based on surveillance systems and is subject to retrospective updates. The methods used (MEM and MSD) are experimental and may be revised, and comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution due to potential changes in testing policy.

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 19 November 2026 (week 47) provides an overview of the health situation in England. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, with 1,826 confirmed cases in hospital settings during week 46. Influenza activity increased, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.4% compared to 8.3% in the previous week. Influenza A positivity rose to 10.1%, while influenza B remained stable at 0.3%. RSV activity also increased, with ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis rising. The report highlights that influenza is circulating above baseline levels and that a briefing note has been issued to the NHS. The data is based on surveillance systems and is subject to retrospective updates. The methods used to determine activity levels, such as the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) and Mean Standard Deviation (MSD), are experimental and may be revised. Testing policies have changed over time, which could affect positivity rates, so comparisons should be made cautiously. The report was published on 19 November 2026, with data up to 15 November 2026.
analysis.summary_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 19 November 2026 (week 47) provides an overview of the health situation in England. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 activity remained stable, with 1,826 confirmed cases in hospital settings during week 46. Influenza activity increased, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.4% compared to 8.3% in the previous week. Influenza A positivity rose to 10.1%, while influenza B remained stable at 0.3%. RSV activity also increased, with ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis rising. The report highlights that influenza is circulating above baseline levels and that a briefing note has been issued to the NHS. The data is based on surveillance systems and is subject to retrospective updates. The methods used to determine activity levels, such as the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) and Mean Standard Deviation (MSD), are experimental and may be revised. Testing policies have changed over time, which could affect positivity rates, so comparisons should be made cautiously. The report was published on 19 November 2026, with data up to 15 November 2026.

title: Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 - Department of Energy (.gov)

analysis.time: Skip to main content An official website of the United States government Here's how you know Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.
analysis.location_and_population: Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website.
analysis.event: Scientists redesigned a hepatitis C drug (boceprevir) to create a more effective treatment for COVID-19, targeting the main protease enzyme (Mpro) that the virus uses to replicate. The Department of Energy reported this development as part of its research initiatives.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The redesigned drug is effective against drug-resistant variants of SARS-CoV-2, including those that resist current therapies like Paxlovid. It targets the Mpro enzyme, which remains consistent across variants, making it a promising treatment option.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research is ongoing, with the redesigned drug being a result of scientific innovation. The Department of Energy is involved in funding and promoting this development, but no specific implementation or distribution details are provided.

analysis.brief_en: The Department of Energy reported on November 18, 2026, that scientists have redesigned a hepatitis C drug, boceprevir, into a more effective treatment for COVID-19. This new drug targets the main protease enzyme (Mpro), which is essential for the virus to replicate and remains consistent across variants. The redesigned drug is effective against drug-resistant strains of SARS-CoV-2, including those that resist existing treatments like Paxlovid. The research was supported by multiple funding sources, including the National Institute of Health and Stanford University. While the development is promising, no specific implementation or distribution details have been provided, and the research is ongoing. This innovation highlights the potential for repurposing existing drugs to address emerging challenges in the fight against the pandemic.
analysis.summary_en: The Department of Energy reported on November 18, 2026, that scientists have redesigned a hepatitis C drug, boceprevir, into a more effective treatment for COVID-19. This new drug targets the main protease enzyme (Mpro), which is essential for the virus to replicate and remains consistent across variants. The redesigned drug is effective against drug-resistant strains of SARS-CoV-2, including those that resist existing treatments like Paxlovid. The research was supported by multiple funding sources, including the National Institute of Health and Stanford University. While the development is promising, no specific implementation or distribution details have been provided, and the research is ongoing. This innovation highlights the potential for repurposing existing drugs to address emerging challenges in the fight against the pandemic.
